title: The mind unshaken
hookLine: the last blessing: a mind the world's ups and downs can touch but not shake

cards: Monday: a compliment from the boss. Tuesday: a client complains. Wednesday: a bonus.
Thursday: a bill twice what you expected. Friday: your post goes semi-viral. Saturday: someone you like unfollows you.
Sunday: a headache. One week, and the mood has ridden up and down like a cheap elevator. Nobody gets to choose which floor the day stops on.
The Mangala Sutta, after company and learning and home and heart, ends with a blessing about exactly that elevator.

teach.b: The poem climbs to its peak in two verses. First: discipline, a pure life, seeing the noble truths, and realizing nirvana. That is the highest blessing.
Then the verse this lesson is named for. Whose mind, when touched by the ways of the world, does not shake. Free of sorrow, free of stain, secure.
That is the highest blessing. The ways of the world have a name in Buddhist teaching: lokadhamma, the worldly conditions. There are eight, in four pairs.

teach.h: EIGHT WINDS: GAIN, LOSS, PRAISE, BLAME
teach.b: Gain and loss. Fame and obscurity. Praise and blame.
Pleasure and pain. Elsewhere the Buddha says these eight come to the untaught person and to the wise disciple alike. Nobody gets only the good half.
The mind is touched. The verse doesn't say the world stops reaching you, or that you stop feeling. Praise still arrives; so does blame.
The difference is that the mind doesn't shake. Like a well-rooted tree in wind: the leaves move, the trunk stays. And then the poem's last verse gathers everything up.
Those who have done these things are undefeated everywhere, and go everywhere in safety.
Theirs is the highest blessing. That's the poem's arc in four days: from the company you keep, to your home, to your heart, to a mind steady enough to stand in any weather. Not luck.
Not omens. A life built so well that the elevator can go up and down, and you can stay standing inside it.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the eight worldly conditions as a daily reflection, and the Mangala Sutta's closing verses are chanted in full at blessings across Theravada countries.

o: the laws a king makes for the world
the teachings meant for lay people only
the worldly winds: gain, loss, praise, blame

games.q: the eight worldly winds: tap the pairs.

s: the verse says the wise are never touched by the world's ups and downs
the mind is touched; it simply does not shake.
the worldly conditions come in four pairs
gain and loss, fame and obscurity, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.
the blessings poem ends with going everywhere in safety
those who live this way are undefeated everywhere and go everywhere in safety.

games.q: your week brings a bonus and a bad review on the same day. the poem's last blessing describes how a steady mind meets them. which?
o: it's touched by both, and doesn't shake.
it celebrates one and hides from the other.
games.why: the verse says the mind is touched by the worldly conditions but does not shake: sorrowless, stainless, secure.

practice: Recall one recent up, a compliment, a win, and let it touch you without grabbing it; then one recent down, a criticism, a loss, and let it touch too, without shoving it away.
Up and down, the winds blow: feel the part of you that stays where it is, the breath, the seat, the steady trunk, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Lokadhamma, the worldly conditions. The last blessing of the Mangala Sutta: touched by gain and loss, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and still not shaken. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali lokadhamma: the worldly conditions, eight in four pairs: gain and loss, fame and obscurity, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.

carryVoice: Your line: unshaken. Touched by every one of the worldly winds, and still standing. Until tomorrow.
